article_title: What the performance of multimodal LLMs on a national licensing exam teaches us about occupational therapy education.
citation: Saita Kazuya, Mine Yuichi, Amano Satoru. (2026). What the performance of multimodal LLMs on a national licensing exam teaches us about occupational therapy education. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-08542-4
title: 60th Japanese National Examination for Occupational Therapists (2025) as an LLM benchmark dataset
description: The 60th JNEOT (February 2025) is a publicly available national licensing exam published by the Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare of Japan, used here as a benchmark for multimodal LLMs. After excluding one officially withdrawn question, "a total of 199 questions were scored, including 177 text-only questions and 22 visually-based questions." Questions span basic sciences and OT-specific content, with 40 practical case-based questions and visual materials such as clinical photographs, CT, MRI and illustrations.
requirements: Official answer keys used as the reference standard; question specialties classified by two researchers with consensus resolution by a third
constraints: The dataset covers a single exam year in Japanese only; categories with small sample sizes (e.g., Rehabilitation Medicine, n = 1) require cautious interpretation
target_learning_goals: assessment of AI capability in professional licensing knowledge
examples: All questions were input into OpenAI o3 between May 3 and 4, 2025, and into the other three models between March 27 and 30, 2025, in a zero-shot manner with no specialized prompt design
key_sources: Saita Kazuya, Mine Yuichi, Amano Satoru. (2026). What the performance of multimodal LLMs on a national licensing exam teaches us about occupational therapy education. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-08542-4

article_title: Motivation and needs of informal physics practitioners
citation: Shams El-Adawy, Alexandra C. Lau, Eleanor C. Sayre, and Claudia Fracchiolla. (2023). Motivation and needs of informal physics practitioners. https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.19040
title: Joint Network for Informal Physics Education and Research (JNIPER)
description: JNIPER is an APS initiative bringing together physicists who facilitate informal physics learning activities and researchers who investigate their impact, aiming to centralize informal learning efforts. It pursues three goals: creating a supportive foundational community, facilitating research-practice partnerships, and supporting adoption of research-based best practices. Its long-term vision is to "elevate the value and recognition for public engagement in physics" through equity-oriented, culturally competent programming.
requirements: A centralized network connecting researchers and practitioners of informal physics education
constraints: Grounded in research, equity, and culturally competent practices as defined by the JNIPER leadership team
target_learning_goals: community building and adoption of research-based informal physics practices
examples: First initiatives launched Fall 2022 include monthly coffee hours and a JNIPER slack channel where members share resources
key_sources: Shams El-Adawy, Alexandra C. Lau, Eleanor C. Sayre, and Claudia Fracchiolla. (2023). Motivation and needs of informal physics practitioners. https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.19040

article_title: Using Jupyter Notebooks to foster computational skills and professional practice in an introductory physics lab course
citation: E. Tufino, S. Oss, and M. Alemani. (2024). Using Jupyter Notebooks to foster computational skills and professional practice in an introductory physics lab course. https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.16675
title: Three-module Jupyter Notebook curriculum for introductory Python data analysis in physics lab
description: A set of eleven Jupyter Notebooks in three modules: an Introduction to Python module (four JNs) covering installation, calculations, plotting, least squares linear regression, correlation and chi-squared; an Application Examples module (five JNs) with exercises such as sunspot moving averages, illuminance vs distance, pendulum period histograms, parabolic motion simulation, and atmospheric CO2 plotting; and an Additional Python Techniques module (two JNs) on data import across Jupyter Lab-Anaconda, Google Colab and online sources. The material is accessible on GitHub and "tailored to be approachable even for students without prior coding experience".
requirements: Notebooks are used both collaboratively in class and independently and asynchronously; students need access to Python environments such as Jupyter Lab-Anaconda or Google Colab
constraints: Designed for first-year introductory laboratory students; some exercises completed asynchronously and independently
target_learners: first-year undergraduate physics majors, including students without prior coding experience
examples: Notebook 4 introduces Pandas and has students analyse a vertically thrown stone's trajectory, testing v2 = 2gh via linearisation, least squares regression and reduced chi-squared.
key_sources: E. Tufino, S. Oss, and M. Alemani. (2024). Using Jupyter Notebooks to foster computational skills and professional practice in an introductory physics lab course. https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.16675

article_title: Informal Education is Essential to Physics: Findings of the 2024 JNIPER Summit and Recommendations for Action
citation: Lau, A. C., Hoehn, J. R., Bennett, M. B., Fracchiolla, C., Hinko, K., Finkelstein, N., and the broader JNIPER Community. (2025). Informal Physics Education Is Essential to Physics: Findings of the 2024 JNIPER Summit and Recommendations for Action. https://www.aps.org
title: JNIPER community of practice for informal physics education
description: JNIPER (Joint Network for Informal Physics Education and Research) is an international community of practice for facilitators, designers, and scholars of IPE, officially formed in Fall 2022 and supported by APS with Michigan State University, University of Colorado Boulder, and the JILA Physics Frontier Center. The paper reports that "Currently, JNIPER has 325 members across over 35 countries, with the majority from the United States". Its community-of-practice elements (Table 1) are domain, community, and practice, enacted through monthly coffee hours, workshops, conference sessions, a professional development program, and online collaboration.
requirements: Communities of practice require a shared domain or goal, supportive relationships among members, and co-created practices, tools, experiences, and methods
constraints: JNIPER supports a global community but is a US-based organization with US-based leadership, so many examples and contexts are US-centric
target_learners: students, post-docs, faculty, staff, public engagement professionals from academic and non-academic institutions
target_learning_goals: effective and impactful ways to engage the public on physics topics and advocacy for informal physics education work
examples: The JNIPER Fellows program trains a small cohort of students in science communication skills, who then produce content for APS Public Engagement programs.
key_sources: Lau, A. C., Hoehn, J. R., Bennett, M. B., Fracchiolla, C., Hinko, K., Finkelstein, N., and the broader JNIPER Community. (2025). Informal Physics Education Is Essential to Physics: Findings of the 2024 JNIPER Summit and Recommendations for Action. https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.18851
